displayQuote: A serious and good philosophical work could be written consisting entirely of jokes

meta.title: Who really said "A serious and good philosophical work could be written consisting entirely of jokes"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Wittgenstein really made this remark — but only as reported by Norman Malcolm in 1958, and the popular wording is a paraphrase, not his own written words.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A serious and good philosophical work could be written consisting entirely of jokes'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Wittgenstein's thought — but reported secondhand by Norman Malcolm (1958), and the famous wording is a later paraphrase.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Wittgenstein really did voice this idea — but the record for it is secondhand: his friend Norman Malcolm reported in his Ludwig Wittgenstein: A Memoir (1958) that Wittgenstein “once said” a serious and good philosophical work could consist entirely of jokes. The neat popular wording “consisting entirely of jokes” is a later paraphrase of Malcolm’s sentence, not a line Wittgenstein himself wrote or published.

source.heading: The source behind the quote

source.excerpt: It is worth noting that Wittgenstein once said that a serious and good philosophical work could be written that would consist entirely of jokes (without being facetious).
trail: The genuine remark comes from Wittgenstein’s friend Norman Malcolm, who wrote that Wittgenstein “once said” such a work could “consist entirely of jokes (without being facetious)” in his 1958 Memoir.
Wikiquote does not file this under sourced Wittgenstein: it places the popular wording in its “Attributed” section, tracing the exact circulating form to a 2004 publication rather than to Malcolm.

One study of the quote’s afterlife argues it is “real, but fake now” — authentically Wittgensteinian, yet usually cited in a paraphrased form detached from its actual source, per The Philosopher’s Meme.
source.excerptNote: Malcolm’s original sentence. Notice it is Malcolm reporting what Wittgenstein “once said” — and it reads “consist entirely of jokes,” not the smoother “consisting entirely of jokes” that now circulates.

source.rightsNote: The line is preserved only in Norman Malcolm’s Ludwig Wittgenstein: A Memoir, first published in 1958 — comfortably within copyright — and the exact popular wording surfaces in later 20th/21st-century publications. Wittgenstein spoke the thought aloud, but there is no pre-1931 or Wittgenstein-authored printed source for it, so it is not public domain.

author.name: Ludwig Wittgenstein
author.heading: About Ludwig Wittgenstein
author.bio: Ludwig Wittgenstein (1889–1951) was among the most influential philosophers of the twentieth century, author of the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (1921) and the posthumous Philosophical Investigations (1953). He worked at Cambridge and was known for gnomic, aphoristic remarks — many of which reach us only through the notebooks and memoirs of students and friends such as Norman Malcolm.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: This is an unusual case: the attribution to Wittgenstein is basically fair, but the way it is quoted quietly misrepresents the record.

items.scope: Presented as Wittgenstein’s own written words
items.why: Wittgenstein never wrote this sentence in any of his books or notebooks. It survives only because Norman Malcolm remembered him saying something like it and wrote it down years later — a secondhand report, not a primary text (Malcolm, Memoir, 1958).

Malcolm’s actual sentence reads “a serious and good philosophical work could be written that would consist entirely of jokes (without being facetious).” The tidy modern version drops the “without being facetious” qualifier and smooths the grammar; Wikiquote logs the circulating form as Attributed, not sourced.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: the joke about jokes is really Wittgenstein’s, but you are quoting Norman Malcolm’s paraphrase of an offhand remark — not a sentence Wittgenstein ever published, per Malcolm’s Memoir.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: The remark is quoted so often because it captures something real about Wittgenstein’s method: his later work proceeds by odd little scenarios, imaginary interlocutors and puzzles that unsettle you into seeing a confusion — more like a comic’s reframes than a treatise’s proofs.
That is exactly why it circulates unchecked. It feels so authentically Wittgensteinian that few readers pause to ask whether he wrote it — and he did not; his friend Norman Malcolm did, from memory.
